(Section)

"Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi asked him ﷺ, saying: 'I made a zihar (a form of divorce in which a husband compares his wife to his mother's back) against my wife until the month of Ramadan ends. One night, while she was serving me, something of her body was exposed to me, and I could not hold back from having intercourse with her.' He ﷺ said: 'Is that what you did, Salamah?' I said: 'Yes, that is what I did. I am patient with the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so judge me by what Allah shows you.' He said: 'Free a slave.' I said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, I do not own any slave other than her,' and I struck the nape of my neck. He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' I said: 'Did I not fall into what I fell into only because of fasting?' He said: 'Then feed sixty poor people a wasq (a measure) of dates.' I said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth as a prophet, we spent the night hungry, having no food.' He said: 'Then go to the official in charge of the charity of Banu Zurayq, and let him give it to you, so you may feed sixty poor people a wasq of dates, and you and your family may eat the rest.' So I returned to my people and said: 'You have shown me hardship and bad judgment, while I found with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ease and good judgment, and he has ordered for me your charity.'" Related by Ahmad.

"Khawlah bint Malik asked him ﷺ, saying: 'Her husband Aws ibn al-Samit made zihar against her,' and she complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was disputing with her about it, saying: 'Fear Allah, for he is your cousin.' She did not leave until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾, and the verses that follow.

He said: 'Let him free a slave.' She said: 'He cannot find one.' He said: 'Then let him fast two consecutive months.' She said: 'He is a very old man and has no strength for fasting.' He said: 'Then let him feed sixty poor people.' She said: 'He has nothing to give in charity.' So he (the Prophet ﷺ) immediately brought a 'araq (a basket) of dates. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I will help him with another 'araq.' He said: 'You have done well. Go and feed sixty poor people with it on his behalf, and return to your cousin.'" Related by Ahmad and Abu Dawud. The wording of Ahmad is: "She said: 'By Allah, it was about me and Aws ibn al-Samit that Allah revealed the beginning of Surat al-Mujadilah.' She said: 'I was with him, and he was an old man whose character had become bad and who was irritable. He entered upon me one day, and I argued with him about something, so he became angry and said: "You are to me like the back of my mother," then he went out and sat in the gathering of his people for a while, then he entered upon me again, and he wanted me for himself.' She said: 'I said: "No indeed, by the One in whose hand is the soul of Khuwaylah, you will not come near me after you have said what you said, until Allah and His Messenger judge about us with a judgment."' She said: 'He overpowered me, but I resisted him, and I overcame him in the way a woman overcomes a weak old man, and I pushed him off me. Then I went out to one of my neighbours, borrowed her clothes, and went out until I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and sat before him, and I mentioned to him what I had suffered from him. I kept complaining to him of his bad character, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kept saying: "O Khuwaylah, your cousin is an old man, so fear Allah concerning him."' She said: 'By Allah, I had not left when the Qur'an was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was overcome by what usually overcame him, then it passed from him, and he said: "O Khuwaylah, Allah has revealed concerning you and your companion," then he recited to me: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 1] up to His saying: ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 4].'

She said: 'Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Tell him to free a slave."'" And he mentioned something similar to what preceded.

In the narration of Ibn Majah: "She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he consumed my youth and I spent my womb for him, until when my age grew old and my children stopped, he made zihar against me. O Allah, I complain to You.' I had not left until Jibril, peace be upon him, came down with these verses."

(Section)

As for "sami'a Allahu liman hamidah" (Allah hears whoever praises Him), al-Suhayli said: The object of sami'a is omitted, because hearing relates to speech and sounds only, not to other things. So the lam remains in its proper function, except that it indicates an additional meaning, namely the response that accompanies hearing. Thus the word combines brevity and an indication of the additional meaning, which is the response to the one who praises Him.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿It may be that some of what you seek to hasten has drawn near to you﴾ (ʿasā an yakūna radifa lakum).

The lam here is not the lam of the object, as they claimed, nor is it superfluous. Rather, radifa is a transitive verb whose governed element is other than this noun, just as the object of sami'a is other than the word in the genitive. The meaning of radifa is "to follow" and "to come after the trace." If you took it to govern the noun in the genitive, the meaning would not be correct when you reflect on it. Rather, the meaning is: "It has followed (radifa) your hastening and your saying," for they said: "When is this promise?" Then the object, which is the saying and the hastening, is omitted, relying on the listener's understanding. The lam indicates the omission, because it prevents the noun it precedes from being an object, and it also indicates another benefit, namely the meaning of "hastened for you" ('ajjala lakum). So it is connected to this meaning, and the sense of the sentence becomes: "Say: it may be that what you seek to hasten has been hastened for you in part," so radifa refers to their saying and their seeking to hasten, and the lam indicates the other meaning. Thus the speech is arranged in the finest order, and brevity combines with completeness of meaning.

I say: The verb sami'a is used in four senses:

The first: hearing as perception, whose object is sounds. From this: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you concerning her husband﴾ and ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of those who said﴾.

The second: hearing as understanding and comprehension, whose object is meanings. From this His saying: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen﴾. The intent is not merely hearing words, but hearing with understanding and intellect. And from this: ﴿We have heard and obeyed﴾.

The third: hearing as response, granting what is asked. From this: "Allah hears whoever praises Him," and in the transmitted supplication: "O Allah, hear (us)," meaning: respond and give what I have asked You.

The fourth: hearing as acceptance and submission. From this His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are listeners to falsehood﴾, meaning they accept it and submit to it without denying it. From this also, according to the more correct of the two opinions: ﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾, meaning receptive and submissive. It was said: they are spies and informants. This is not correct, for spies and informants are only used between two separate groups, and so they are needed; but this verse concerns the hypocrites, who were mixed among the Companions, so they had no need of spies and informants.

Given this, the hearing of perception transitively takes its object directly. The hearing of acceptance takes the lam at times and min at other times. This depends on the meaning: when the context requires acceptance, it is followed by min, and when it requires submission, it is followed by lam.

As for the hearing of response, it takes the lam, as in "Allah hears whoever praises Him," because it implies the meaning of istajaba lahu (responded to him), and there is no omission there; rather it is an implied meaning. As for the hearing of understanding, it transitively takes its object directly, because what it implies transitively takes its object directly.

If it is said: what do you say about the words of one who makes zihar (a pronouncement likening one's wife to his mother's back), "You are to me like the back of my mother": is it an inshā' (performative utterance) or a ikhbār (informative statement)?

If you say it is an inshā', it is invalid for several reasons:

The first: an inshā' does not admit of being affirmed or denied. Yet Allah, glorified is He, has here denied them in three places.

The first of these is in His saying, «they are not their mothers» (58:2). He negated what they affirmed, and this is the very essence of denial. One who divorces his wife would not properly be described as "she is not his divorced wife."

The second is in His saying, «And indeed they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood» (58:2). An inshā' cannot be an objectionable word; rather, the objectionable thing is the informative statement.

The second reason: He called it zūr (falsehood), and zūr is lying. When Allah has called them liars, this shows that zihar is an ikhbār and not an inshā'.

The third: zihar is forbidden, and the only ground for its prohibition is that it is a lie.

The evidence for its prohibition is five things:
The first: He described it as munkar (objectionable).
The second: He described it as zūr (falsehood).
The third: that expiation (kaffārah) was prescribed for it. Had it been permissible, there would be no expiation for it.
The fourth: Allah said, ﴿That is what you are admonished with﴾ (65:2?). Admonition occurs only regarding impermissible matters.
The fifth: His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ (58:2). Pardon and forgiveness occur only regarding a sin.

If you say it is an ikhbār, that is invalid for several reasons:

The first: zihar was a divorce (ṭalāq) in the pre-Islamic period, and Allah made it, in Islam, a prohibition that is lifted by expiation. This is agreed upon among the scholars. Had it been an informative statement, it would not have caused prohibition: if it were true, this is obvious; and if it were false, it would be even further from being a cause for prohibition.

The second: the wording of zihar itself, by its own nature, necessitates its legal ruling, which is prohibition. This is the very essence of an inshā', unlike an ikhbār, which does not by itself necessitate its ruling. Thus, denying that it is an inshā' while affirming the essence of inshā' in it is combining two contradictories.

The third: the effect of the words "You are to me like the back of my mother" in producing prohibition is like the effect of "You are free," "You are divorced," "I have sold you," "I have pawned you," "I have married you," and the like, in producing their rulings. So how can they say these are inshā's but zihar is not? What is the difference?

It is said: As for the jurists, they say zihar is an inshā'. Some later scholars disputed this, and said: the correct view is that it is an ikhbār.

He responded to what they argued from its being an inshā'.

He said: As for their saying, "It was a divorce in the pre-Islamic period": this does not imply that they used to establish divorce by it; rather, it implies that they used to remove the marital bond by uttering it.

So its removal could be because it is an inshā', as you claim, or because it is a lie, and it was their custom that whoever reports this lie has his marriage bond removed. This is like their rule that a she-camel becomes forbidden when she bears ten offspring, and similar things.

He said: As for your saying that it necessitates a temporary prohibition, and this is the essence of an inshā' and not of an ikhbār, then we do not grant that there is any prohibition at all. What the Qur'an indicates is the obligation to put expiation before intercourse, just as purification is put before prayer. When the Lawgiver says, "Do not pray until you have purified yourself," this does not indicate that prayer is forbidden to one who is impure; rather, that is a kind of ordering.

Even if we grant that a prohibition follows from zihar, the prohibition following a thing may be because the wording necessitates it and indicates it, and this is the inshā'. Or it may be a pure punishment, like the ordering of the deprivation of inheritance following killing. Killing is not an inshā' of the prohibition; and like the ordering of ta'zīr (discretionary punishment) following lying, and the removal of uprightness ('adālah) by it. This is an ordering by legal stipulation, not by the implication of the wording.

The essence of an inshā' is that the wording was established for that ruling and indicates it, like the formulas of contracts. So the causality of speech is more general than its being a cause through inshā' or otherwise. Every inshā' is a cause, but not every cause is an inshā'. So causality is more general, and its general form cannot be used as evidence for inshā'. The more general does not necessitate the more specific. Thus the difference between the prohibition following divorce and its following zihar becomes clear.

He said: As for your saying that it is like uttering divorce, emancipation, sale and the like, this is an analogy regarding causes, so we do not accept it. And even if we granted it, the text of the Qur'an rejects it.

These objections against them are invalid.

As for his saying that its being a divorce in the pre-Islamic period does not imply that they used to establish divorce by it, etc., this is a statement that is certainly invalid. For they did not intend to report a lie so that prohibition would follow from it; rather, when they wanted divorce, they used the wording of zihar intending divorce. They did not consider themselves liars or reporters; they were only creating divorce by it. This is why it continued in the early days of Islam, until Allah abrogated it by expiation in the case of Khawlah bint Tha'labah, who was married to 'Ubādah ibn al-Ṣāmit. He (her husband) said to her, "You are to me like the back of my mother."

She came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about that. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "She has become forbidden to him."

She said, "O Messenger of Allah, by Him who sent down the Book to you, he did not mention divorce, and he is the father of my children and the dearest of people to me." He said, "She has become forbidden to him."

She said, "I complain to Allah of my poverty and loneliness." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "I do not see you except as one who has become forbidden to him, and I have not been commanded about your case with anything." She kept returning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and whenever he said to her, "She has become forbidden to him," she cried out and said, "I complain to Allah of my poverty and the severity of my condition, and that I have young children; if I gather them to him, they will be lost, and if I gather them to me, they will go hungry."

She kept raising her head to the sky, saying, "O Allah, I complain to You."

This was the first zihar in Islam. Then revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the revelation ended, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Call your husband." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to him the saying of the Most High: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the one who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah, and Allah hears your dialogue﴾ (58:1), and the verses.

This shows that zihar was in the early days of Islam an inshā' of the prohibition resulting from divorce, and then that was abrogated by expiation. With this, his analogy with the prohibition of the she-camel when she bears ten offspring and similar things becomes invalid. For there is no inshā' wording there that necessitates prohibition; rather, it is a legislation by them for this prohibition upon this cause.

As for his saying, "We do not grant that it necessitates a prohibition," this is an invalid statement. For there is no dispute among the jurists that zihar necessitates a prohibition that is lifted by expiation. So if he has intercourse with her before expiating, he is sinful by the well-known consensus (ijmā') of the religion. And the temporary prohibition here is like the prohibition by iḥrām (pilgrim's state), by fasting, and by menstruation.

As for his analogy with prayer while in a state of purity, it is corrupt. For Allah obligated the one who prays to pray with purity. If he does not come with purity, he has abandoned what Allah obligated upon him, and so he deserves sin. But the one who makes zihar has forbidden his wife to himself and likened her to one who is forbidden to him. So Allah prevented him from approaching her until he expiates. Here there is a prohibition based on an expiation. In prayer, nothing is accepted without purity, because it is an unlawful prayer in the first place.

As for his saying: the prohibition following a thing may be because the wording necessitates it, or it may be a punishment, etc.: its answer is that these two are not mutually exclusive in zihar. For it is forbidden, and the woman becomes forbidden by it with a temporary prohibition until he expiates. This does not prevent the wording from being an inshā', like the combining of three divorces according to those who hold that they take effect, and divorce during menstruation: it is forbidden and the prohibition follows it. And you have said that the divorce of an intoxicated person takes effect as a punishment for him, although he did not intend to create a cause by which his wife is divorced, by consensus.

So the prohibition being a punishment does not negate that it is attributed to its causes, which are inshā's of it.

As for his saying: causality is more general than inshā':

Its answer is that cause is of two kinds: an act and a statement. Whenever it is a statement, it is only an inshā'. If you mean by generality that the causality of statement is more general than its being an inshā' or an ikhbār, this is disallowed. And if you mean that absolute causality is more general than its being causality through act or through statement, this is granted, but it does not benefit you at all.

The decisive matter is: his saying, "You are to me like the back of my mother," contains both inshā' and ikhbār.

It is an inshā' insofar as he intends prohibition by this wording, and an ikhbār insofar as it likens her to his mother's back.

For this reason Allah called it "an objectionable word and a falsehood."

So it is objectionable in respect of its being an inshā', and falsehood in respect of its being an ikhbār.

As for his saying: the objectionable (munkar) is the false informative statement, from nukr, and nukr is more general than that:

The denial (inkār) occurs in both the inshā' and the ikhbār, for it is the opposite of what is known (ma'rūf). So whatever has not been permitted in inshā' is objectionable, and whatever is not true in ikhbār is falsehood.

[The ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning zihar, and an explanation of what Allah revealed about it, and the meaning of return (ʿawd) that necessitates expiation]

Allah, the Most High, says: ﴿Those of you who pronounce zihar from their wives, they are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them. And indeed, they utter an objectionable word and a falsehood. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving. And those who pronounce zihar from their wives and then retract what they said, then (the penalty is) the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished with, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do. But whoever cannot find (a slave), then fasting for two consecutive months before they touch one another. But whoever is unable, then feeding sixty needy people. That is so you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. And those are the limits of Allah, and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ (58:2–4).

It is established in the Sunan and the Masānīd: that Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit made zihar from his wife Khawlah bint Mālik ibn Tha'labah, and she is the one who argued with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning it and complained to Allah, and Allah heard her complaint from above the seven heavens. She said, "O Messenger of Allah, Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit married me when I was young and desired. When my years had passed and I had borne him children, he made me like his mother in his sight." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to her, "I have nothing regarding your matter." She said, "O Allah, I complain to You."

It is also related that she said, "I have young children; if he takes them to himself, they will be lost, and if I take them to myself, they will go hungry." Then the Qur'an was revealed.

And 'Ā'ishah said: "Praise be to Allah, who has encompassed all voices with His hearing. Khawlah bint Tha'labah came complaining to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I was in a corner of the house, and some of her speech was hidden from me. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Allah has heard the speech of the one who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah, and Allah hears your dialogue; indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing﴾."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let him free a slave." She said: "He cannot find one." He said: "Then let him fast two consecutive months." She said: "O Messenger of Allah, he is an old man who has no ability to fast." He said: "Then let him feed sixty needy people." She said: "He has nothing of anything to give in charity." She said: "Then at that moment a basket of dates was brought." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I will help him with another basket." He said: "You have done well. Feed sixty needy people on his behalf, and return to your cousin."

In the Sunan it is related that "Salamah ibn Ṣakhr al-Bayāḍī made zihar from his wife for the duration of the month of Ramadan, then he had intercourse with her one night before its end. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'Is that so, O Salamah?'"

He said: I said: "It is so, O Messenger of Allah, twice, and I am patient with the command of Allah. So judge me by what Allah has shown you." He said: "Free a slave." I said: "By Him who sent you with the truth as a prophet, I do not own a slave other than her," and I struck the side of my neck. He said: "Then fast two consecutive months." I said: "Did I fall into what I fell into except through fasting?" He said: "Then feed a wasq of dates to sixty needy people."

I said: "By Him who sent you with the truth, we have spent the night hungry, having no food." He said: "Go to the official of the charity of Banū Zuraiq, and let him give it to you, and feed sixty needy people a wasq of dates, and eat the rest yourself and your dependents."

He said: So I went back to my people and said: "I found among you narrowness and bad judgment, and I found with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) abundance and good judgment, and he has commanded me regarding your charity."

In the Jāmi' of al-Tirmidhī, from Ibn 'Abbās: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) who had made zihar from his wife and had intercourse with her. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I made zihar from my wife and had intercourse with her before I expiated.' He said: 'What led you to that, may Allah have mercy on you?' He said: 'I saw her anklet in the light of the moon.' He said: 'Then do not approach her until you do what Allah has commanded you.'"

He said: This is a hadith that is ḥasan, gharīb, ṣaḥīḥ.

And in it also: from Salamah ibn Ṣakhr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning one who makes zihar and has intercourse before expiating, he said: "One expiation (only)." And he said: ḥasan, gharīb. End of quote. In its chain there is a break between Sulaymān ibn Yasār and Salamah ibn Ṣakhr.

In the Musnad of al-Bazzār, from Ismā'īl ibn Muslim, from 'Amr ibn Dīnār, from Ṭāwūs, from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I made zihar from my wife, then I had intercourse with her before I expiated.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did Allah not say: ﴿before they touch one another﴾ (58:3)?'

He said: 'I was seduced.' He said: 'Refrain from her until you expiate.'"

Al-Bazzār said: "We do not know of it being related with a better chain than this, although Ismā'īl ibn Muslim has been criticized, and a large group of people of knowledge have related from him."

These rulings thus include several matters.

The first: the abolition of what they used to practice in the pre-Islamic period, and in the early days of Islam, of zihar being a divorce, even if he stated the intention for it by saying, "You are to me like the back of my mother, meaning by it divorce," it would not be a divorce but zihar. This is by consensus, except for some rare disagreement. Aḥmad, al-Shāfi'ī and others have explicitly stated this. Al-Shāfi'ī said: "If he makes zihar intending divorce, it is zihar; or if he divorces intending zihar, it is divorce." This is his wording, so it is not permissible to attribute to his school anything contrary to this. Aḥmad stated that if he says, "You are to me like the back of my mother, meaning by it divorce," it is zihar and she is not divorced by it. This is because zihar was a divorce in the pre-Islamic period, and it was abrogated, so it is not permissible to return it to the abrogated ruling.

Also, Aws ibn al-Ṣāmit only intended by it divorce in the way it was in the past, and the ruling applied to it was that of zihar, not divorce.

Also, it is explicit in its ruling, so it is not permissible to make it a metaphor (kināyah) in the ruling which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, abolished by His legislation. The decree of Allah is more worthy, and the judgment of Allah is more binding.

Among the rulings in this verse: zihar is forbidden and it is not permissible to commit it, because, as Allah has informed us about it, it is an abhorrent statement (munkar min al-qawl) and a falsehood (zur), and both are prohibited. The difference between the aspect of it being munkar and the aspect of it being zur is that his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" includes his report about her with that and his creating (insha') its prohibition upon her. Thus it includes both a report and a performative act: the report is a falsehood (zur), and the performative act is abhorrent (munkar). Zur is falsehood, the opposite of established truth, and munkar is the opposite of what is recognized as good (ma'ruf). Allah, glorified is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾ [al-Mujadila: 2], and in this there is an indication of the existence of the cause of sin, which, were it not for Allah's pardon and forgiveness, He would have held the person accountable for.

Another ruling: expiation (kaffarah) is not obligatory by the mere act of zihar; rather, it becomes obligatory only by return (al-'awd).

This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). Al-Thawri narrated from Ibn Abi Najih, from Tawus, who said: "If he speaks zihar, it has become binding upon him." This is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from him. Ma'mar narrated from Tawus, from his father, regarding Allah's saying: ﴿Then they return from what they said﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3], that he said: "He makes her upon him like the back of his mother, then he returns and has intercourse with her, so [the expiation is] freeing a slave."

People have related from Mujahid that expiation is obligatory by the mere act of zihar; Ibn Hazm related this from al-Thawri and Uthman al-Batti. These scholars were not unaware that return (al-'awd) is a condition for expiation, but for them, return means returning to what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah of zihar-ing, like Allah's saying regarding the penalty for hunting: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], meaning he returned to hunting after its prohibition was revealed. For this reason He said: ﴿Allah has pardoned what has passed﴾.

They said: Because expiation was only obligatory in exchange for what he uttered of munkar and zur, which is zihar itself, not intercourse or the intention to it. They also said: Because when Allah, glorified is He, prohibited zihar and forbade it, return would be the doing of what was forbidden, as He said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return, We will return﴾ [al-Isra': 8], meaning: if you return to sin, We return to punishment. So return here is the very act of what was forbidden.

They also said: Because zihar was a divorce (talaq) in the Jahiliyyah, so its ruling was transferred from divorce to zihar, and expiation was prescribed for it, along with the prohibition of the wife until he makes expiation. This necessitates that its ruling be determined by its wording, just as with divorce.

The majority disputed this and said: return (al-'awd) is a matter beyond the mere utterance of zihar, and it is not valid to interpret the verse as referring to a return to it in Islam, for three reasons:

First: this verse explains the ruling for one who makes zihar in Islam, which is why it uses the verb in the present tense: "yuzahiruna" (they make zihar). Since this is an explanation of the ruling for zihar in Islam, by your reckoning it is itself the return, so how can He say after it: "Then they return," while the meaning of this return, according to you, is other than zihar?

Second: if return were what you mentioned, and the present tense had the meaning of the past, the sense would be: "Those who made zihar from their wives and then returned in Islam." Expiation would then be obligatory only upon one who made zihar in the Jahiliyyah and then returned in Islam. From where, then, do you make it obligatory upon one who began zihar in Islam without returning? Here there are two matters: a prior zihar and a return to it, and this would completely nullify the ruling of zihar now, unless you make "yuzahiruna" refer to one occasion and "ya'udun" to another, with the present tense standing in for the past. That contradicts the structure of the text and departs from eloquence.

Third: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded Aws ibn al-Samit and Salamah ibn Sakhr to make expiation, and did not ask them whether they had made zihar in the Jahiliyyah or not. If you say: nor did he ask them about the return which you make a condition, and if it were a condition he would have asked them about it.

It is said: As for one who takes return to be the mere continuation of withholding (al-imsak) after zihar for a period of time during which divorce can occur, this follows his own view and is the very basis of his argument. As for one who takes return to be intercourse and intention, he says: the context of the story clearly shows that those who made zihar intended intercourse, and only refrained from it; this will be explained later, if Allah wills.

As for zihar being munkar from the word and zur, yes, it is so; but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only made expiation obligatory for this munkar and zur by two matters: by the act itself and by the return, just as the ruling of ila' is only consequent upon it together with intercourse, not upon either one alone.

[Section: the claim of the Zahiriyyah that the meaning of return is restating the wording]

The majority said: expiation is not obligatory except by return after zihar. Then they differed regarding the meaning of return: is it restating the very wording of zihar, or is it something beyond that? There are two positions. The people of the Zahir (Zahiriyyah) all said: it is restating the wording of zihar, and they did not relate this from any of the early generation (salaf) at all; it is a view that none of them preceded them in, although this kind of complaint hardly any school of thought is free from.

They said: Allah, glorified is He, did not make expiation obligatory except for zihar that is repeated, not for zihar that is initiated. They said: The argument from the verse is in three aspects.

First: the Arabs do not understand, in their languages, return to a thing except doing its like a second time. They said: This is the Book of Allah and the speech of His Messenger and the speech of the Arabs between us and you. Allah said: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

This is the parallel of the verse in that the verb "return" is followed by the preposition "li" (to), meaning their doing again a second time the same as what they did first. And Allah said: ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾ [al-Isra': 8], meaning: if you repeat the sin, We repeat the punishment. From it is His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret counsel, then they return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8]. This is in the very surah of zihar, and it clarifies the intended meaning of return in it, for it is its parallel in act and in intention, and the reference is recent in being mentioned.

They said: Also, what they said is the wording of zihar; so return to speech is uttering it a second time, and the Arabs understand nothing other than this.

They said: Also, what is other than repetition of the wording is either withholding, or resolve, or action, and none of these is speech, so performing it is not a return, neither in wording nor in meaning; and because resolve, intercourse, and withholding are not zihar, so performing them is not a return to zihar.

They said: If return were intended as going back on what one had prohibited oneself, as one says "he returned in the gift" (a'ada fi al-hibah), he would have said: "Then they return concerning what they said," as in the hadith: "The one who takes back his gift is like the one who returns to his vomit."

Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm argued with the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that Aws ibn al-Samit had a condition of madness (lamam), and whenever his madness intensified he would make zihar from his wife, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed concerning him the expiation of zihar.

He said: This necessitates repetition, without doubt.

He said: And nothing is authentic regarding zihar except this report alone.

He said: As for your censure of us that this view was not held by any of the Companions, show us from the Companions one who said that return is intercourse, or resolve, or withholding, or that it is return to zihar in the Jahiliyyah, even from a single man among the Companions; you will never be more fortunate with the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ than we are.

[Section: the majority's refutation of the Zahiriyyah]

The majority disputed this and said: The meaning of return is not the restating of the first wording; for if that were the return, he would have said: "Then they repeat what they said," because one says "he repeated his speech exactly" (a'ada kalamahu bi-'aynihi). As for "'ada," it is used with actions, as one says "he returned to his action" ('ada fi fi'lihi), "in his gift" (fi hibatihi); this is its usage with "fi." And one says "'ada ila 'amalihi" (returned to his work), "ila wilayatihi" (to his office), "ila halihi" (to his state), "ila ihsanihi wa isa'atihi" (to his goodness and his wrongdoing), and similar, and "'ada lahu" also.

As for speech, one says "a'adahu" as when "Dimad ibn Tha'labah said to the Prophet ﷺ: a'id 'alayya kalimatika" (repeat for me your words).

And as when "Abu Sa'id said: a'idha 'alayya ya Rasul Allah" (repeat them to me, O Messenger of Allah).

And this is not necessarily so, for one says "a'ada maqalatahu" (he repeated his statement) and "'ada limaqalatihi" (he returned to his statement), and in the hadith: "fa'ada limaqalatihi" (so he returned to his statement), with the same meaning as "a'adaha," without difference. And more corrupt than this is the refutation of those who answered them by saying that repeating speech is impossible, like repeating yesterday, for it is not possible for two times to be combined.

He said: This is in the utmost corruption, for repeating speech is of the same kind as repeating an act, which is bringing the like of the first, not the same thing. And it is strange that a partisan says: the dissent of the Zahiriyyah is not to be considered, yet debates with them using such discussions and refutes them with such a refutation. Likewise, the refutation of those who answered them with the parallel of "the one who returns in his gift," for it is not the parallel of the verse; its parallel is: ﴿Have you not seen those who were forbidden from secret counsel, then they return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8]. Yet this verse clarifies the intended meaning of the zihar verse, for their return to what they were forbidden is their coming back to the very thing forbidden, which is the secret counsel, and the intended meaning is not repeating that same secret counsel exactly, but their returning to the thing forbidden. Likewise His saying regarding zihar: ﴿then they return to what they said﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3], meaning: to their saying. It is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, which is the prohibition of the wife by likening her to the forbidden. So return to the prohibited is return to it, and that is his doing it; this is the basis for those who said it is intercourse.

The crux of the matter is that the saying concerns the meaning of what is said, and what is said is the prohibition; and returning to it is returning to it, which is making it lawful again for oneself after its prohibition. This accords with the rules of the Arabic language and its usage, and this is what the majority of the early generation (salaf) and later generations (khalaf) held, as Qatadah, Tawus, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Malik, and others said. Nothing is known from any of the early generation that interpreted the verse as restating the wording at all, neither from the Companions, nor the Successors, nor those after them.

Here there is a matter that escaped those who took it to be restating the wording: return to an action necessitates departing from the state one is now in and returning to the state one was in first, as Allah said: ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾ [al-Isra': 8]. Do you not see that their return is departing from the goodness they were in and returning to wrongdoing? And like the poet's saying:

"And if he returns to goodness, return is most praiseworthy."

The state he is now in is prohibition by zihar, and the state he was in is permissibility of intercourse by marriage, which causes lawfulness. So the return of the one who made zihar is a return to the lawfulness he had before zihar, and that is what necessitates expiation. So reflect on this. Return requires a thing to which one returns after departing from it. The secret of the difference between return in a gift and return to what the zihar-maker said has become clear: a gift is a thing, a specific object, and returning to it includes bringing it back into his ownership and his disposal of it as before, unlike the zihar-maker, who, by the prohibition, has left the marital relation, and by the return has sought to go back to the state he was in with her before the prohibition. So the most fitting expression is to say "'ada li-kadha," meaning "'ada ilayhi" (returned to it).

In the case of a gift one says "'ada ilayha" (returned to it), and the Prophet ﷺ commanded Aws ibn al-Samit and Salamah ibn Sakhr with the expiation of zihar, and they did not utter it twice, for they did not report that about themselves, nor did their wives report it about them, nor did any of the Companions, nor did the Prophet ﷺ ask them: "Did you say that once or twice?" Such a matter, had it been a condition, he would not have neglected to explain it.

The secret of the matter is that return includes two things: a thing one returns to, and a thing one returns from, and both are necessary. What one returns from includes annulling and nullifying it; what one returns to includes preferring it and wanting it. So the return of the zihar-maker necessitates annulling zihar and nullifying it, and preferring its opposite and wanting it. This is exactly the understanding of the early generation of the verse: some say return is coitus (al-isabah), some say intercourse (al-wat'), some say touching (al-lams), and some say resolve (al-'azm).

As for your statement that it is only the repeated zihar on which expiation is obligatory: if you mean by it the repeated wording, that is a claim according to what you have understood; and if you mean by it the zihar in which the zihar-maker has returned to what he said, this does not necessitate the repetition of the first wording.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 58, verse 2 (part 3 of 3):

As for the hadith of ʿAʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) concerning the zihar of Aws ibn al-Samit, how sound it is, and how far its implication is from your school's position.

[Section: Whoever is unable to perform the expiation, it does not fall from him]

Among these rulings: whoever is unable to perform the expiation, it does not fall from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) assisted Aws ibn al-Samit with a basket (ʿaraq) of dates, and his wife assisted him with the same amount until he performed the expiation. He also commanded Salama ibn Sakhr to take the charity (ṣadaqa) of his people and expiate with it on his own behalf. Had it fallen away through inability, he would not have commanded them to pay it; rather, it would remain as a debt upon him. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi and one of the two narrations from Ahmad.

A group held that it falls away through inability, just as obligations fall away when a person is unable to perform them and their substitutes.

Another group held that the expiation of Ramadan does not remain in his obligation but falls away, whereas the other expiations do not fall away. This is what Abu al-Barakat Ibn Taymiyya affirmed as sound.

Those who held that it falls away argued that if it were obligatory despite inability, it would not be given to him, for a man cannot be a recipient of his own expiation, just as he cannot be a recipient of his own zakat. The proponents of the first view say: if he is unable and another pays on his behalf, it is permissible to give it to him, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) gave the expiation of the one who had intercourse during Ramadan to him and his household, and just as he permitted Salama ibn Sakhr and his household to eat from his expiation which he had paid on his behalf from his people's charity. This is the school of Ahmad, with a single narration from him concerning the expiation of one who had intercourse with his wife in Ramadan, and with two narrations from him concerning the other expiations. The Sunna indicates that if he is unable to pay the expiation and another pays it on his behalf, it is permissible to give his expiation to him and to his household.

If it is said: Is it permissible for him, if he is poor, has dependents, and is owed zakat which he needs, to take it for himself and his dependents? It is said: No, this is not permissible, because the obligatory payment is not made by him; rather, the imam or the zakat collector may give his zakat to him after it has been collected from him, according to the more sound of the two narrations from Ahmad. If it is said: Is it permissible for him to waive it from himself? It is said: There is no text on this, and the difference between the two is clear.

If it is said: If the master permits his slave to expiate by manumission, may he free himself? It is said: The narrations differ regarding the case where he has permitted him to expiate by wealth, whether he may shift from fasting to it, according to two narrations. One of them: he is not permitted to do so, and his obligation is fasting. The second: he is permitted to shift to it, and he is not obliged to. The prohibition is for the right of the master, and he has given permission for it. If we say that he may do so, then may he manumit? The narrations from Ahmad differ on this, and there are two narrations from him on the matter. The reasoning for prohibition is that he is not of the people who hold wala' (clientage rights), and manumission depends on wala'. Abu Bakr and others chose that he may manumit. On this basis, may he free himself? There are two opinions within the school. The reasoning for permissibility is the absolute nature of the permission; the reasoning for prohibition is that permission to manumit is understood to refer to freeing others, just as if he had been permitted to give charity, the permission would be understood as applying to charity to others.

[Section: It is not permissible to have intercourse with the one one has made zihar with before expiation]

Among these rulings: it is not permissible for the one who has made zihar to have intercourse with the woman before expiation. Here, the scholars differed on two points. The first: whether he may engage in lesser intimacy short of intercourse before expiation or not. The second: if his expiation is by feeding, may he have intercourse before it or not? On both questions there are two opinions among the jurists, which are two narrations from Ahmad and two opinions of al-Shafiʿi.

The reasoning for prohibiting enjoyment short of intercourse is the apparent sense of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿before they touch one another﴾ [al-Mujadila: 3]; and because He likened her to one whose intercourse is forbidden and to its preliminaries. The reasoning for permissibility is that "touching" (tamassa) is a metaphor for intercourse, and the prohibition of intercourse does not necessitate the prohibition of its preliminaries, for a menstruating woman's intercourse is forbidden but not its preliminaries, a fasting person is forbidden intercourse but not its preliminaries, and a captive woman's intercourse is forbidden but not its preliminaries. This is the view of Abu Hanifa.

As for the second question, namely intercourse before expiation when it is by feeding: the reasoning for permissibility is that Allah, Glorified is He, restricted the expiation to being before touching in the case of manumission and fasting, and left it unrestricted in the case of feeding. Each has its wisdom. Had He intended the restriction for feeding, He would have mentioned it as He mentioned it for manumission and fasting. He, Glorified is He, did not restrict this and leave that unrestricted in vain, but for an intended benefit, and there is no benefit except restricting what He restricted and leaving unrestricted what He left unrestricted. The reasoning for prohibition is deriving the ruling of what He left unrestricted from what He restricted, either by way of clarification according to the sound view, or by analogy in which the distinguishing factor between the two cases has been removed, and He, Glorified is He, does not differentiate between two alike. He mentioned ﴿before they touch one another﴾ twice; had He repeated it a third time, the speech would have been lengthened. By mentioning it twice He drew attention to the recurrence of its ruling in the expiations. Had He mentioned it only once at the end of the speech, it would have given the impression that it was specific to the last expiation; had He mentioned it only at the first occurrence, it would have given the impression that it was specific to the first. Repeating it with every expiation would be prolixity, and what occurred was the most eloquent, most forceful and most concise form of speech. Furthermore, He drew attention to expiating before touching by fasting, despite its long duration and the strong need for intimacy with a wife; so requiring it to precede feeding, which does not take long, is more fitting.

[Section: The expiation is not given except to the needy, and the poor are included among them]

Among these rulings: it is not sufficient to give the expiation except to the needy (masakin), and the poor (fuqara') are included among them, just as the needy are included in the term "poor" when used absolutely. Our companions and others generalized the ruling to everyone who takes from zakat due to need, and they are four: the poor, the needy, the wayfarer, and the debtor for the sake of a public interest, and the mukatab (slave contracted for freedom). The apparent sense of the Qur'an is that it is restricted to the needy, so it does not extend beyond them.

[Section: The expiation does not fall away by intercourse before expiation, nor is it multiplied]

Among these rulings: the expiation does not fall away by intercourse before expiation, nor is it multiplied; rather, it remains as one expiation, as the ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) which has preceded indicates. Al-Salt ibn Dinar said: I asked ten jurists about the one who has made zihar and has intercourse before expiating, and they said: one expiation. He said: they were al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, Masruq, Bakr, Qatada, ʿAta', Tawus, Mujahid, and ʿIkrima. He said: the tenth, I think, was Nafiʿ. This is the view of the four imams.

It is reported authentically from Ibn ʿUmar and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs that he owes two expiations. Saʿid ibn Mansur mentioned from al-Hasan and Ibrahim, concerning one who makes zihar and then has intercourse with her before expiating: he owes three expiations.

He also mentioned from al-Zuhri, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Abu Yusuf that the expiation falls away.

The reasoning for this is that its time has passed, and there remains no way to pay it before touching.

The answer to this is that the passing of the time of performance does not cancel an obligation in the person's liability, as with prayer, fasting, and all other acts of worship. The reasoning for the obligation of two expiations is that one is for the zihar accompanied by return (ʿawd), and the second is for the forbidden intercourse, like intercourse during the day in Ramadan, and like the intercourse of one in ihram. There is no known basis for requiring three, unless it is a punishment for his daring to commit what is forbidden. The ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indicates contrary to these opinions. And Allah knows best.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 58, verse 5:

Al-kabt (humiliation, disgrace, and being thrown down on the face) means abasement, shame, and being prostrated on the face.

Al-Nadr and Ibn Qutaybah said: it is rage and grief.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "kubitū" means they were destroyed, disgraced, and grieved. If the one who opposes (Allah and His Messenger) is kabtan (brought low), then, were he safe for his own self and his wealth, he would not be kabtan; rather he would be joyful and delighted, healing his chest from Allah and His Messenger, safe for his blood and his wealth. Where, then, is the kabt?

And this is supported by His saying: ﴿They will be humiliated just as those before them were humiliated﴾. So their fear is of a humiliation like the humiliation of those before them, which is destruction, either from Him or at the hands of His servants and His allies.

(Benefit)

Companionship (al-ma'iyyah) is of two kinds:

First, general companionship, which is the companionship of knowledge and encompassing (al-ihatah). An example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4].

And His saying: ﴿There is no secret conference of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them, nor of less than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7].

Second, specific companionship, which is the companionship of nearness (ma'iyyat al-qurb). An example is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [al-Nahl: 128].

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153].

And His saying: ﴿And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾ [al-Ankabut: 69].

This is the companionship of nearness, which includes allegiance (al-muwalah), support (al-nasr), and protection (al-hifz).

Both meanings are a companionship from Him toward the servant, but the first is a companionship of observation and encompassing, while the second is a companionship of allegiance, support, and assistance.

In the language of the Arabs, "ma'a" (with) denotes fitting companionship; it does not imply mixing, intermingling, nor being adjacent or distant.

Whoever imagines from it any of these meanings has misunderstood and been afflicted by his own misunderstanding.

As for nearness (al-qurb): it is not expressed in the Qur'an except as specific.

It is of two kinds: His nearness to the one who calls upon Him, by answering him; and His nearness to His worshipper, by rewarding him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 58, verse 10:

It is related in the authentic collection (al-Sahih) from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he used to say in his supplication:

"O Allah, I seek refuge in You from anxiety and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from the burden of debt and from being overpowered by men."

So the Prophet (ﷺ) sought refuge from eight things, each two of which are paired:

Anxiety (al-hamm) and grief (al-huzn) are paired, and they are the pain that comes upon the heart. If it concerns what has passed, it is grief (huzn); if it concerns what is yet to come, it is anxiety (hamm). The pain that arises from the loss of the past leaves the trace of grief, and the pain that arises from fear of what is coming leaves the trace of anxiety.

Incapacity (al-ajz) and laziness (al-kasal) are paired. If the benefit of the servant is missed and kept far from him, then if it is from lack of ability it is incapacity (ajz), and if it is from lack of will it is laziness (kasal).

Cowardice (al-jubn) and miserliness (al-bukhl) are paired. Beneficence gladdens the heart, expands the breast, brings blessings and repels calamities, while abandoning it brings humiliation and constriction and prevents blessings from reaching him. Thus cowardice is the abandonment of beneficence with the body, and miserliness is the abandonment of beneficence with wealth.

The burden of debt (dal' al-dayn) and being overpowered by men (ghalabat al-rijal) are paired, for the subjugation and domination that befall the servant come either from himself or from others.

And if you wish, you may say: either by right or by wrong, from others.

The point is that the Prophet (ﷺ) made grief among the things one seeks refuge from.

This is because grief weakens the heart, enfeebles resolve and harms the will, and nothing is more beloved to Satan than the grief of the believer. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Secret counsel is only from Satan, that he may grieve those who believe﴾ [al-Mujadila: 10].

So grief is a sickness of the hearts which prevents it from rising, proceeding and exerting itself. The reward for it is the reward of the afflictions that the servant is tested with involuntarily, such as sickness, pain and the like.

As for it being an act of worship that one is commanded to acquire and seek, that is not so. There is a difference between what the servant is rewarded for among the things commanded, and what he is rewarded for among the trials. However, what is praiseworthy in grief is its cause, its source and its consequence, not its essence. For the believer either grieves over his failure and shortcoming in serving his Lord and in worship,

or he grieves over his entanglement in disobedience and sin and the squandering of his days and hours.

This indicates the soundness of faith in his heart and the life of his heart, since it occupies his heart with such pain so that he grieves over it. Had his heart been dead, he would not feel this, nor grieve, nor suffer pain, for there is no pain for a dead thing from a wound. The more alive his heart is, the stronger his feeling of this pain will be. But grief does not benefit him,

for it weakens him, as has preceded.

Rather, what benefits him is to proceed on the journey, to strive, to exert himself and to expend his effort. This is like one who has been separated from his companions on a journey, who sits on the road grieved and dejected, witnessing his separation and talking to himself about catching up with the people.

Whenever he tires and grieves, he tells himself that he will catch up with his companions, and promises it that if it is patient it will join them, and the loneliness of separation departs from it. Thus is the wayfarer to the abodes of the righteous and the dwellings of those brought near. More specific than this grief is his grief over wasting time through divided attention that weakens the heart from the completeness of its journey and striving on its path, for division of attention is one of the greatest trials for the wayfarer, especially at the beginning of his affair. The first is grief over failure in deeds; this is grief over the deficiency of his state with Allah, the dividing of his heart, how it has become a vessel for the division of his state, and the occupation of his heart with other than its Worshipped One.

More specific than this grief is his grief over a part of his heart, how it is empty of the love of Allah, and over a part of his body, how it is turned toward what Allah does not love. This is the grief of the elite, and it includes their grief over every obstacle that occupies them from what they are engaged in, whether a passing thought, a will, or a preoccupation from outside.

These levels of grief are unavoidable on the path, but the discerning person is one who does not let them possess him and keep him seated, but instead replaces the thought of them with the thought of what will repel them. For when something disliked comes upon the soul, if the soul is small, it becomes occupied with thinking about it and about its occurrence, diverting from thinking about the means by which it may be repelled, and this bequeaths grief to it. If the soul is great and noble, it does not dwell on it, but directs its thought to what benefits it. If it knows an exit from it, it thinks about the way to that exit and its causes; and if it knows there is no exit from it, it thinks about servanthood to Allah within it. This becomes a substitute for grief for it. In every case, there is no benefit at all for it in grief. And Allah knows best.

(Subtle point)

Allah, glorified is He, has informed in His Book of the raising of ranks in four places:

The first is this verse: ﴿Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees.﴾

The second is His saying: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely. [They are] those who establish prayer and from what We have provided them, they spend. Those are the believers, truly. For them are degrees with their Lord and forgiveness and noble provision.﴾

The third is the Exalted's saying: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds, for them are the high degrees.﴾ (20:75)

The fourth is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And Allah has preferred those who strive [with their wealth and lives] over those who sit [at home] by a great reward — degrees from Him and forgiveness and mercy.﴾ (4:95–96)

These are four places. In three of them, the elevation by degrees is for the people of faith, which is beneficial knowledge and righteous action. The fourth is elevation through jihad. Thus all the elevations in degrees return to knowledge and jihad, by which the religion is established.

(Section)

Through the chain of Kathir ibn Abdullah, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger, as it began. So blessed are the strangers." It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, who are the strangers?" He said: "Those who revive my Sunnah and teach it to the servants of Allah." And it used to be said: "The scholars are strangers because of the multitude of the ignorant."

Then it is mentioned from Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, regarding His saying: ﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ (6:83), that he said: "By knowledge." And Ibn Abbas, regarding Allah's saying: ﴿Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees﴾, said: "Allah will raise those among the believers who have been given knowledge above those who have not been given knowledge by degrees."

And he said in (Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah):

al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, Salamah ibn Raja narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Hamid narrated to us, al-Qasim narrated to us, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili who said: Two men were mentioned to the Messenger of Allah, one of them a scholar and the other a worshipper. The Messenger of Allah said: "The excellence of the scholar over the worshipper is like my excellence over the least of you."

Then the Messenger of Allah said: "Indeed Allah, His angels, the people of the heavens and the earth, even the ant in its hole and even the fish in the sea, send blessings upon those who teach people good."

al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hadith that is ḥasan gharib.

I heard Abu Ammar al-Husayn ibn Hurayth al-Khuza'i say: I heard al-Fudayl ibn Iyad say: "A scholar who acts and teaches is called great in the kingdom of the heavens."

This is also narrated from the Companions. Ibn Abbas said: "The scholars of this Ummah are two men: a man whom Allah has given knowledge and he disseminates it to people and does not take a price for it, nor does he buy with it a price. Those, the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea, the beasts of the earth and the noble scribes send blessings upon them. And a man whom Allah has given knowledge but he withholds it from His servants and takes a price for it and buys with it a price; that one will come on the Day of Resurrection bridled with a bridle of fire."

Ibn Abd al-Barr mentioned it as marfu', but there is doubt about its being traced to the Prophet.

As for his saying: "Indeed Allah, His angels, and the people of the heavens and the earth send blessings upon the teacher of people good": since his teaching people good was a cause of their salvation, their happiness and the purification of their souls, Allah repaid him in kind by placing upon him, from His blessings and the blessings of His angels and the people of the earth, what would be a cause of his salvation, his happiness and his success.

Also, since the teacher of people good was manifesting the religion of the Lord and its rulings, and making known to them His names and attributes, Allah placed upon him, from His blessings and the blessings of the people of His heavens and His earth, what would be an honouring of him, an ennobling of him and a manifestation of praise for him among the people of the heavens and the earth.

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Abu al-Darda, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah say:

"Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge therein, Allah will make easy for him a path to Paradise. Indeed the angels lower their wings in pleasure for the seeker of knowledge. Indeed the scholar is asked forgiveness by whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, even the fish in the water. The excellence of the scholar over the worshipper is like the excellence of the moon over the rest of the stars. Indeed the scholars are the heirs of the prophets. Indeed the prophets did not bequeath dinar or dirham; they bequeathed only knowledge, so whoever takes it has taken a abundant share."

It was also narrated by al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Khalid ibn Yazid, from Uthman ibn Ayman, from Abu al-Darda, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever goes out in the morning seeking knowledge that he learns, Allah opens for him by it a path to Paradise, the angels spread their wings for him, the angels of the heaven and the fish of the sea send blessings upon him. The scholar's excellence over the worshipper is like the excellence of the full moon's night over the rest of the stars. The scholars are the heirs of the prophets; indeed the prophets did not bequeath dinar or dirham, they bequeathed only knowledge, so whoever takes knowledge has taken his portion. The death of a scholar is a calamity that cannot be repaired, a breach that cannot be closed, a star that is extinguished; the death of a tribe is easier than the death of a scholar."

This is a hadith ḥasan. The path which he treads to Paradise is a reward for his treading in this world the path of knowledge that leads to the pleasure of his Lord. The angels' lowering of their wings for him is out of humility, reverence and honouring for what he carries and seeks of the inheritance of prophethood. It indicates love and esteem. From the angels' love for him and their esteem is that they lower their wings for him, because he is seeking that by which the life and salvation of the world comes. Therein is a resemblance to the angels, and between him and them there is affinity, for the angels are the most sincere and most beneficial of Allah's creation to the children of Adam. Through them every happiness, knowledge and guidance came to them. And from their benefit to the children of Adam and their sincerity is that they seek forgiveness for their wrongdoers, praise their believers, help them against their enemies from the devils, and are keen on the servant's interests many times over his own concern for his self; rather they wish for him from the good of this world and the Hereafter what the servant does not wish and what does not occur to his mind, as some of the Successors said: "We found the angels the most sincere of Allah's creation toward His servants, and we found the devils the most deceitful of creation toward the servants." And the Exalted said: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire. Our Lord, and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You promised them and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants. Indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise. And protect them from evil deeds, and whoever You protect from evil deeds that Day—You have had mercy upon him. And that is the great achievement."﴾ (40:7–9)

What sincerity to the servants is like this, except the sincerity of the prophets?

So when the servant seeks knowledge, he has striven in the greatest thing by which the servants of Allah are advised; therefore the angels love him and esteem him, even lowering their wings for him out of pleasure, love and exaltation.

Abu Hatim al-Razi said: I heard Ibn Abi Uways say: I heard Malik ibn Anas say: the meaning of the Messenger of Allah's saying "lower their wings" is: they spread them out in supplication for the seeker of knowledge instead of hands.

Ahmad ibn Marwan al-Maliki said in his book al-Mujalasah: Zakariyya ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Basri narrated to us, saying: I heard Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb say: We were with some narrators in Basra, and he narrated to us the hadith of the Prophet that the angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge. In the assembly with us was a man from the Mu'tazilah who began to mock the hadith and said: "By Allah, tomorrow I will nail my sandals with nails and step on the wings of the angels with them." He did so, and walked in the sandals, and both his feet dried up and gangrene fell upon them.

al-Tabarani said: I heard Abu Yahya Zakariyya ibn Yahya al-Saji say: We were walking in some alleys of Basra toward the door of some narrators, and we hurried our pace, and with us was a man, dissolute in his religion, who said: "Lift your feet from the wings of the angels; do not break them," mocking. He did not leave his place until both his feet dried up and he fell.

In the Sunan and the Masanid, from the hadith of Safwan ibn Assal: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have come seeking knowledge." He said: "Welcome to the seeker of knowledge. Indeed the seeker of knowledge, the angels surround him and shade him with their wings, and they ride upon one another until they reach the lowest heaven, out of their love for what he seeks."

(A great benefit)

The best of what souls acquire and hearts attain, by which the servant gains elevation in this world and the Hereafter, is knowledge and faith. For this reason He, glorified is He, joined them in His saying: ﴿Those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have remained according to the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection."﴾ (30:56)

And His saying: ﴿Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge by degrees.﴾

These are the essence and core of existence and those qualified for lofty ranks. But most people are heedless regarding the true reality of the names knowledge and faith, by which happiness and companionship are attained. And regarding their reality, to the extent that each group thinks that what it possesses of knowledge and faith is that by which happiness is attained. It is not so; rather most of them have neither a faith that saves nor a knowledge that elevates. Rather they have blocked for their souls the paths of knowledge and faith which the Messenger brought and to which he called the Ummah, and upon which he and his Companions after him were, and those who followed them in their method and traces.

So every group believed that knowledge is what they have, and rejoiced, and ﴿they cut up their affair among themselves into sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has﴾ (23:53).

Most of what they have is speech, opinions and conjecture, and knowledge lies beyond speech. As Hammad ibn Zayd said: I said to Ayyub: "Is knowledge more today or in what came before?" He said: "Speech is more today, and knowledge in what came before is more."

So this well-grounded scholar distinguished between knowledge and speech. Books are very numerous, and speech, argument and mental constructs are numerous, but knowledge is far removed from most of them, and it is what the Messenger brought from Allah. The Exalted said: ﴿Whoever argues with you about it after the knowledge has come to you﴾ (3:61). And He said: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge﴾ (2:145). And He said about the Qur'an: ﴿It was sent down with His knowledge﴾ (4:166), meaning: in it is His knowledge.

When the time since this knowledge grew long, the matter came to such a state that many people took the stirrings of thoughts, the passing impulses and opinions as knowledge, and set books for them, and spent their breaths upon them, wasting time in them, filling pages with ink and hearts with darkness. So much so that many of them declared that there is no knowledge in the Qur'an and Sunnah, and that their proofs are verbal and do not give certainty or knowledge. The devil shouted this word among them and announced it in their midst until the nearest of them made the farthest hear it, and hearts slipped out of knowledge and faith as a snake slips out of its skin, or a garment from its wearer.

The Imam, the scholar Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim said: Some of our companions told me about some followers of the followers of these people's students, that he saw him occupied with some of their books without having memorized the Qur'an, and he said to him: "If you had first memorized the Qur'an, it would have been better." He said: "Is there knowledge in the Qur'an?"

Ibn al-Qayyim said: One of the leaders of these people said to me: "We only listen to hadith for the sake of blessing, not to benefit knowledge from it, because others have spared us this burden, so our reliance is on what they understood and established." Without doubt, whoever has this as the extent of his knowledge is, as the poet said:

"They alighted in Mecca among the tribes of Hashim, / and I alighted in al-Batha, the farthest place."

He said: My shaykh once said, describing these people, that they circled the masters of schools and so attained the lowest of goals. And it is enough of a proof for you that what they possess is not from Allah: look at the contradictions and conflicts in it and the collision of parts with parts. The Exalted said: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much contradiction﴾ (4:82). This indicates that what is from Him, glorified is He, has no contradiction, and what has contradiction and conflict is not from Him. How can opinions, imaginings and passing thoughts become a religion by which one is obligated and by which judgment is made upon Allah and His Messenger? Glory be to You, this is a great slander.

The knowledge of the Companions, which they discussed, was other than the sciences of these disputing, guessing people, as al-Hakim related in the biography of Abu Abd Allah al-Bukhari: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, when they gathered, would only discuss the Book of their Lord and the Sunnah of their Prophet; there was no opinion or analogy among them. And the poet spoke well:

"Knowledge is 'Allah said,' and 'His Messenger said,' / the Companions said; it is not deception.
What knowledge is it that you set up for disagreement, foolishness, / between the Messenger and the opinion of a jurist?
Nay, nor denial of the attributes or their negation, / out of fear of likening or assimilation."

(Section)

As for faith, most people, or all of them, claim it: ﴿And most people, even if you were eager, are not believers﴾ (12:103).

Most believers have only general faith.

As for detailed faith in what the Messenger brought—knowledge, affirmation, acknowledgment, love, and knowledge of its opposite, with aversion and hatred for it—this is the faith of the elite of the Ummah and the special ones of the Messenger. It is the faith of al-Siddiq and his party. Many people's share of faith is acknowledgment of the existence of the Creator and that He alone created the heavens and the earth and what is between them. The idolaters of Quraysh and others did not deny this.

Others regard faith as merely uttering the two testimonies, whether or not it is accompanied by deeds, and whether or not it agrees with the heart's assent or contradicts it.

Others regard faith as merely the heart's assent that Allah, glorified is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, even if he does not confess with his tongue and does nothing at all. Indeed, even if he reviles Allah and His Messenger and commits every grave sin, while believing in the oneness of Allah and the prophethood of His Messenger, he is a believer.

Others regard faith as the denial of the attributes of the Lord, the Exalted: His elevation above His Throne, His speaking with His words, His Books, His hearing, His sight, His will, His power, His volition, His love and His hatred, and other things by which He described Himself and by which His Messenger described Him.

Thus, for them, faith is the denial and rejection of all the realities of this, and adherence to what the opinions of the bewildered and the conjectures of the guessers dictate. These are people who refute one another and whose statements nullify one another, and they are, as ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Imam Aḥmad said:

"Divided about the Book, opposing the Book, and agreed upon abandoning the Book."

Others, for them, faith is worshipping God according to their spiritual tastes, their ecstatic experiences, and what their souls desire, without being bound by what the Messenger brought.

Others hold that faith is following what they found their fathers and forebears upon, by way of conformity, whatever that may be. Rather, their faith is built upon two premises:
The first: that this is the saying of our forebears and fathers.
The second: that whatever they said is the truth.

Others, for them, faith is noble character, good dealing, cheerful countenance, thinking well of everyone, and leaving people to their heedlessness.

Others, for them, faith is detachment from the world and its attachments, emptying the heart of it, and asceticism toward it. So when they see a man like this, they regard him as one of the masters of the people of faith, even if he is stripped of faith in knowledge and in action. Higher than these are those who make faith nothing but knowledge, even if it is not accompanied by action.

All of these have not known the reality of faith, nor have they upheld it, nor has it upheld them. They are of several kinds: among them are those who make faith that which contradicts faith; among them are those who make faith that which is not regarded as part of faith; among them are those who make it a condition of faith that does not suffice for its attainment; among them are those who require for its establishment that which negates and opposes it; and among them are those who require of it that which is not of its nature in any respect.

Faith lies beyond all of that. It is a composite reality made up of: knowledge of what the Messenger brought; assent to it in the heart as conviction; affirmation of it by the tongue; submission to it in love and humility; acting upon it inwardly and outwardly; implementing it and calling to it to the extent possible; and its perfection lies in loving for God's sake, hating for God's sake, giving for God's sake, withholding for God's sake, and that God alone be one's deity and object of worship.

The path to it is singling out the following of His Messenger, outwardly and inwardly, and closing the eye of the heart against turning toward anything other than God and His Messenger.

And success is from God.
